curation.lead:
Leon D. Black (born July 31, 1951) is an American billionaire financier and co-founder and former CEO of Apollo Global Management. Between 2013 and 2017, Black paid Jeffrey Epstein approximately $158 million in advisory fees routed primarily through Southern Trust Company, Inc., an Epstein-controlled U.S. Virgin Islands entity [Finding #1460][Finding #1382]. The payment schedule was documented by the Dechert LLP investigation commissioned by Apollo's Conflicts Committee and filed as an SEC 8-K exhibit on January 25, 2021 [SEC:0001193125-21-016405][Finding #1460]. The work covered estate and tax planning, art advisory, trust restructuring, and advisory coordination across Black's family financial architecture [Finding #1486]. Payments began with $23.5 million in 2013 under a signed service agreement for addressing a structural defect in a 2006 GRAT that the Dechert investigation described as carrying an estimated $500 million estate tax liability [Finding #1571][Finding #1409]. Subsequent payments of $70 million (2014), $30 million (2015), and $8 million (2017) were made ad hoc, with no payment in 2016 following a fee dispute [Finding #1382]. Separately, Black loaned Epstein $30.5 million in early 2017 through BV70 LLC for a purported art transaction; Epstein repaid only $10 million before his death [Finding #1576].

The advisory relationship extended beyond conventional financial consulting. Epstein served as vice president and secretary of the Leon Black Family Foundation from approximately 2010 to 2012 — after his 2008 Florida conviction — and, by October 2015, maintained a 25-item work program across personal, philanthropic, and Apollo-adjacent matters [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_023291][Finding #6]. Over a dozen outside advisory firms, including Paul Weiss, PricewaterhouseCoopers, McDermott Will & Emery, Macfarlanes, and Apollo's in-house legal function, fed into an arrangement with Epstein as the coordination point [Finding #1486]. DOJ Volume 11 calendar entries document in-person meetings between the two men multiple times per month from at least 2010 through June 2019, including after Epstein's 2008 conviction and continuing through November 2016 [Finding #9].

The Dechert report found "no evidence that Epstein ever introduced Black, or offered to introduce Black, to any underage woman," and acknowledged that compensation "far exceeded any amounts Black paid to his other professional advisors" [Finding #1460]. The Manhattan District Attorney's office (DANY) separately investigated Black on trafficking allegations connected to Epstein, identifying at least three victims represented by Wigdor LLP partner Jeanne Christensen; DANY ultimately closed its investigation as to Black and he was not criminally charged [Finding #10]. Black stepped down as Apollo CEO in March 2021 and was succeeded by Marc Rowan. A civil sexual assault lawsuit, Doe v. Black (1:23-cv-06418, SDNY), filed July 25, 2023, remains pending as of February 2026, with an appeal before the Second Circuit (25-564) [Finding #1384]. Black has reduced his Apollo holdings from 67.8 million shares in January 2022 to approximately 4.5 to 7 million shares through sales and gifts.

sections.title: The $158 Million Payment Structure
sections.content:
The financial relationship between Leon Black and Jeffrey Epstein is preserved in a 21-transaction ledger attached as Exhibit A to the Dechert LLP report filed with Apollo's January 2021 8-K [EFTA00027019][Finding #1583]. Payments began on February 15, 2013, when Black transferred $15 million to Southern Trust Company as the first installment under a signed service agreement; a second installment of $8.5 million followed on October 15, 2013 [Finding #1409][Finding #1382]. The Dechert investigation described this initial $23.5 million as compensation for what it called "the most valuable piece of work Epstein provided Black" — identifying and addressing a structural defect in a 2006 Grantor Retained Annuity Trust that Dechert assessed as carrying an estimated $500 million estate tax exposure [Finding #1571]. The defective GRAT had been established by a trusts and estates attorney whom Epstein had earlier recommended to Black [Finding #1571].

An additional $26.5 million was paid later in 2013 under a second, unsigned agreement, bringing total 2013 payments to $50 million [Finding #1382]. The 2014 payments reached $70 million, paid ad hoc rather than under formal agreement, including $20 million attributed to a "step-up basis transaction" [Finding #1382][Finding #1460]. The 2015 payments totaled $30 million; no payments were made in 2016 following a fee dispute; and a final $8 million was paid in April 2017 for tax advisory and compliance work, producing the confirmed $158 million total [Finding #1382][Finding #1460]. Exhibit A documents 21 transactions flowing from Leon and Debra Black personally, Black Family Partners LP, Narrows Holdings LLC, and BV70 LLC to Southern Trust Company, with smaller amounts to Gratitude America Ltd and Plan D LLC, and each transaction carries Deutsche Bank-SDNY Bates numbers [Finding #1583][Finding #3].

Payment routing obscured both payer and recipient on specific transactions. The October 2015 payment of $19.75 million was split: $15 million to Southern Trust Company via Black Family Partners account 0135, and $4.75 million to the J Epstein VI Foundation directed through an "automotive LLC" — a single-member Black-owned LLC ordinarily used for automobile purchases — described in internal correspondence as routed that way to "avoid public disclosure of Leon name" [Finding #219][EFTA02339486]. Richard Kahn instructed Brad Wechsler (CEO of Black's family office) on the routing, and the automotive entity required an inter-company loan from either Black's personal account or LDB 2014 LLC to fund the $4.75 million because it lacked sufficient cash [Finding #219]. The initial $19.75 million amount had been negotiated down from an earlier $15 million Southern Trust + $4.75 million foundation formulation after Black told Wechsler "full 19.75mm shld go to a charitable fndn" [Finding #220]. Dechert reported that Black was under the "misconception" that the payments were tax-deductible — paying in "sixty cent dollars" — based on representations Epstein made to him [Finding #1460].

sections.title: Epstein's Scope of Control Over Black's Finances
sections.content:
Epstein's access to Black's financial affairs was broad. A House Oversight document dated October 27, 2015 sets out a 25-item work program across personal, corporate, and philanthropic files: "1 phaidon 2 new trustee 3 art partnership 4 grats 5 art space 6 regan arts 7 plane restructure refinance 8 boat restructure 9 estate plan refresh 10 TRA review sale 11 BRH doc review 12 sale of stock/art 13 gifts of art 14 charity pledges 15 cash flow 16 new IT/personnel 17 operational redo 18 debra/children involvement 19 tax plan disclosures gaming foreign apollo and phaidon related 20 investments rationalize 21 bank loans consolidate 22 consolidate/reduce entities 23 outside consultants 24 review legal bills 25 Bens house alex films" [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_023291]. A separate May 2015 document describes the advisory scope as "investment, PE, real estate, publishing, grats, tra, brh (death), foundation, museum, tax projections cash flow projections, coordination with tax from apollo" [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_023222]. The "(death)" notation on BRH refers to modeling the consequences of a founder's death for the BRH partnership structure that underpins Apollo Global Management voting control [Finding #1585].

Epstein received detailed financial reports on Black Family Partners LP, the central family holding partnership, which managed approximately $1.95 billion in assets as of June 30, 2013 and held 92,717,166 Apollo Operating Group shares [Finding #8]. BFP partners included Leon Black personally (7.4%), the Black 2006 Family Trust (71.5%), the 1997 Black Family Trust (9.2%), the Judah 2009 Trust (4.7%), LDB 2011 LLC (7.2%), and additional trusts [Finding #8]. Richard Joslin, CFO of Elysium Management LLC (Black's family office at 445 Park Avenue, Suite 1401), routinely sent Epstein trust accounting summaries, charity commitment lists, cash flow projections, art valuations, password-protected tax returns, and GRAT annuity schedules [Finding #7][Finding #1503]. Ada Clapp, Elysium's Chief Legal Officer, sent Epstein the Administrative Services Agreement between Elysium and APO1 Trust along with the GRAT agreement, initial funding assignment, annuity payment chart, and Empire Valuation invoices [Finding #1503]. Brad Wechsler, Elysium's CEO, corresponded with Epstein on Athene capital calls, Phaidon credit facilities, and BFP entity structures [Finding #7][Finding #1464].

A House Oversight document [HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_023355] lists the outside advisory network Epstein coordinated: Paul Weiss, McDermott Will & Emery, Macfarlanes (UK), PricewaterhouseCoopers, Reich (accounting), Withers Bergman, Empire Valuation Consultants, Akin Gump, BDO Seidman, and "Apollo in house," which Finding #1486 reads as confirming coordination with Apollo's internal tax and legal function [Finding #1486]. Epstein described the pre-existing posture as "many outside counsel with little or no coordination" [Finding #1486]. Analysis of this multi-firm role, as set out in Finding #1486, offers one explanation for both the size of the $158 million fee and the observed difficulty of replacing him. When the arrangement deteriorated, Epstein wrote to a correspondent: "nuts. he needs to replace wechsler, joslin, castrucci. its WAAAYY overdue. paralized him" [Finding #1574] — a characterization internal to Epstein's own correspondence.

sections.title: Apollo and the Co-Founder Tax Exposure
sections.content:
Epstein's advisory work for Black extended to matters affecting all three Apollo Global Management co-founders — Black, Joshua Harris, and Marc Rowan — through the BRH Holdings partnership structure [Finding #1574][Finding #1585]. BRH Holdings GP Ltd, a Cayman Islands exempted company owned and controlled by all three founders, held the single Class B share of Apollo Global Management LLC, which controlled 79.7% of voting power post-IPO while representing no economic interest; BRH Holdings LP was the underlying partnership through which the founders held their economic interests [Finding #1585]. All three founders were required to file IRS Form 8865 (Return of U.S. Persons With Respect to Certain Foreign Partnerships) annually for BRH Holdings LP [Finding #1574].

In August 2016, Epstein identified a compliance gap: he had been filing Form 8865 for Black since 2013, but the filings were inaccurate, and Harris and Rowan had never filed at all, leaving open statutes of limitation extending back to at least 2007 [EFTA02452148][Finding #1574]. Epstein discussed the matter with Brad Karp at Paul Weiss, who responded: "First I have heard of this" [Finding #1574]. Epstein proposed filing three or six years back under the IRS delinquent international disclosure program, and by September 29, 2016 Apollo's Suzanne Wong was coordinating with Deloitte to complete historical 8865 data back to 2007 by the end of October [Finding #1574]. The correspondence shows Epstein had direct involvement in the foreign-partnership tax affairs of all three Apollo founders, not just Black, and Paul Weiss — through Karp as chairman — was drawn into remediation for the full group rather than Black alone [Finding #1574][Finding #1486].

This multi-founder posture is relevant to how the Dechert report should be read. The Dechert investigation was commissioned by Apollo's Conflicts Committee and framed its inquiry around Black's personal relationship with Epstein [Finding #1460]. The HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_023355 advisory-ecosystem document and the 8865 sequence together show Paul Weiss, Akin Gump, PwC, and Apollo's in-house tax function coordinating through Epstein on matters spanning all three founders — not only Black [Finding #1486][Finding #1574]. Analysis of that correspondence indicates that a scope limited to Black's personal advisory bill understates the degree to which Apollo's in-house legal function and Paul Weiss were integrated into Epstein-coordinated work for the founder group as a whole [Finding #1486][Finding #1574].

Financial Trust Company, an Epstein entity, separately purchased 263,257 shares of Apollo Global Management stock during its March 2011 IPO through a "directed share offering program managed by the lead broker-dealer" [Finding #1383]. The shares, worth approximately $5 million at the IPO price of roughly $19 per share, were later transferred to Southern Financial LLC in 2013 and held through at least September 2019 [Finding #1383]. The Dechert report stated "Apollo never did any business with Epstein"; a directed share allocation through the lead broker-dealer and IPO underwriting process is a carve-out from the general share pool that the issuer typically authorizes, and Black said he did not recall the transaction when questioned nearly a decade later [Finding #1383][Finding #1460]. The Athene investment was another point of direct Epstein access: a December 2014 BFP LP cash flow projection shows a $41.6 million Athene capital call as the largest projected disbursement, with projected cash going negative by May 2015 [Finding #1464]. Joslin communicated Athene investment details directly to Epstein, who separately asked Wechsler and Kahn which entity held "the athene investment on the books" [Finding #1464].

sections.title: Brad Karp and Paul Weiss
sections.content:
Brad Karp, chairman of Paul Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison LLP, corresponded directly with both Black and Epstein on matters spanning Black's personal finances and the Apollo founders' tax exposure [Finding #528][Finding #1574]. On March 3, 2016, Karp asked Paul Weiss partner Bruce Birenboim: "I have been asked by Leon if we can have a $2m escrow fund established at the firm, from which payments would be made monthly pursuant to a contract with an individual. Leon would pay any and all costs and indemnify the firm against any claims" [Finding #528][EFTA02470157]. Birenboim declined, citing firm policy against acting as escrow agent outside standard real estate transactions, and Karp forwarded the exchange to Epstein [Finding #528]. The identity of the unnamed "individual" who would have received monthly payments from the escrow fund has not been established in the available record [Finding #528].

DOJ records show joint conference calls with Epstein, Black-related parties, Karp, Brad Wechsler, and Akin Gump's Patrick Fenn. A November 2016 three-way billing email among Karp, Epstein, and Black addressed which party was paying for Paul Weiss, Akin Gump, Deloitte, and PwC services, placing Epstein's advisory fees and Paul Weiss's legal fees in a single billing structure [Finding #1486]. When Epstein identified the 8865 filing failure affecting all three Apollo founders in August 2016, he brought it to Karp first [Finding #1574]. Separately, Epstein invoked the David Petraeus scandal as a cautionary analogy when advising Black through Karp, comparing Black's use of an Apollo employee as intermediary to the Petraeus-Broadwell situation [EFTA02372647]. The Paul Weiss memorandum submitted on Black's behalf to Senator Ron Wyden, Chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, addressed the scope of the Black-Epstein relationship [Finding #10]. Paul Weiss partner Alan Halperin also served as outside counsel managing the APO1 GRAT structures [Finding #1503].

sections.title: Family Office and Entity Architecture
sections.content:
Black's financial life was organized through Elysium Management LLC, his family office at 445 Park Avenue, Suite 1401, New York [Finding #7]. Key personnel included Brad Wechsler (CEO), Richard Joslin (CFO), Barry J. Cohen (President and Special Counsel), Ada Clapp (Chief Legal Officer), Melanie Spinella (Executive Assistant to Black at Apollo), Eileen Alexanderson (Black Family Partners LP), John Castrucci, and Larry Delson (attorney) [Finding #7]. Epstein received tax returns, financial reports, art valuations, trust documents, and password-protected files from Elysium staff on a routine basis [Finding #7][Finding #1503]. An internal entity list sets out the "Global Black family" architecture: LDB, AIF Management, BJAV Marine Ltd, Narrows Holdings I and II, ILIT #2, BFP LP, APO1 Agreement, LBF Holdings LLC, APO1 GRATs 1-7, Black Family 1997 Trust, Black Family 1997 GST Exempt Trust, SH Meadow Lane LLC, OFH LLC, LDB 2011 LLC, ASB 2011 Trust, BEB 2011, BV70 LLC, JMWT LLC, Pent Holdings Inc, and NY 70th Street LLC [EFTA01919502][Finding #1594].

The APO1 GRAT cascade anchored the estate plan. The system used at least eight sequential Grantor Retained Annuity Trusts (GRATs 1 through 8) funded with Black Family Partners LP interests that contained Apollo Operating Group units [Finding #1569][Finding #1503]. BFP LP held 92,717,166 APO shares, annuity payments were made quarterly (Jan/Mar/Apr/Jun/Jul/Sep/Oct/Dec rather than Feb/May/Aug/Nov), and in-kind BFP interests received as annuity payments were re-GRATed into successor trusts [Finding #1569]. Empire Valuation Consultants LLC prepared fair market value appraisals, applying discounts for lockup restrictions that decreased from 27% at outset; a June 2015 annuity valued at $98,780,916 was one data point in that sequence [Finding #1569]. The CLAT (Charitable Lead Annuity Trust) structure diagrammed in EFTA02726259 shows a two-step estate plan in which assets flow to a CLAT producing an annuity stream to the Leon Black Family Foundation, with the remainder passing to Heritage Trust [Finding #30].

Phaidon Global LLC, a Black publishing and media vehicle held through the trust structure, received at least a $10 million line of credit from BFP LP established in August 2013, and Epstein received Phaidon financial reports, valuations (including a GBP 11.2 million 2015 valuation), tax returns, and strategic planning material covering expansion into art investments, film, insurance, and internet publishing [Finding #13]. BV70 LLC, owned by Black, served as a vehicle for two sets of transactions. In October 2015, BV70 transferred $10 million to Gratitude America Ltd, capitalizing that entity's money market account [Finding #1576]. In March and April 2017, BV70 made two loans to Epstein's Plan D LLC totaling $30.5 million — $22.5 million on March 31 and $8 million on April 17 — described as connected to an "art transaction involving Epstein" [Finding #1576]. Deutsche Bank AML Compliance flagged the $22.5 million wire, noting it could not find any information about BV70 LLC online and asking "What is the purpose? What is the relationship? What products/services does BV70 LLC provide?" [EFTA01385659][Finding #1576]. Black demanded full repayment in early 2018; Epstein repaid only $10 million, leaving $20.5 million unpaid at his death [Finding #1576]. The Yggdrasil Trust, another Black family trust, separately transferred $2,204,718.75 on April 29, 2015, to National Bank of Delaware County for an account labeled "Luxury Catalogs" with reference "Dante's Commedia" — an art acquisition routed through the trust architecture, with the wire initiated by Joann Perrone and referencing Mayra Johnson [Finding #19]. A 2014 Southeast Asian Art inventory for Narrows Holdings lists bronze sculptures with stock numbers E0598, E0853, and EX320 among others, and Epstein recommended art consultants including George Goldner from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and managed an Art Partnership position on Black's books [Finding #20].

sections.title: Philanthropic Flows and Gratitude America
sections.content:
Black operated two foundations at the 445 Park Avenue address through Elysium Management: the Debra and Leon Black Family Foundation (EIN 13-3947890, established 1998, NTEE T20Z) and the Leon D. Black Foundation (EIN 20-5117734, established 2007, NTEE A33 arts) [Finding #5]. The Family Foundation was the primary grant-making vehicle, with revenue of $12.14 million and expenses of $11.76 million in 2014 [Finding #5]. Its 2014 recipients included $750,000 approved for the Clinton Foundation, $1.5 million for Birthright Israel Foundation, and $1 million for Harlem Village Academies. Additional grants from 2016 through 2019 included $500,000 to Clinton Foundation entities, $500,000 to Tony Blair Foundation entities, $2 million to Memorial Sloan-Kettering, and $1.5 million to Harvard College. The foundation's 2019 board included Apollo executives John Hannan (Director) and Barry Cohen (Director/Treasurer), both listed care of Apollo Global Management.

The largest documented Epstein-directed philanthropic flow involves Gratitude America Ltd. The Dechert report confirmed Black donated $10 million to Gratitude America in October 2015, describing it as "a charitable organization affiliated with Epstein," and recorded Black's stated reason: that he "understood that Epstein was a strong proponent of scientific innovation" [Finding #1524][Finding #4]. The donation flowed through BV70 LLC [Finding #1576]. A separate letter from Gratitude America to Black dated August 21, 2015 thanked him for a $5 million donation, but Dechert found no bank record or Family Office document confirming this additional payment [Finding #1524]. Gratitude America, controlled by Richard Kahn, subsequently granted $225,000 to Black's own Melanoma Research Alliance — a partial round-trip in which $225,000 of Black's donation to an Epstein-affiliated entity was redirected to a Black-affiliated charity [Finding #4]. The Family Foundation's grant pattern collapsed post-scandal: revenue dropped from $3.82 million in 2019 to effectively zero by 2023 ($1 in revenue, $3,680 in expenses, $85,000 in assets), consistent with a wind-down. The Leon D. Black Foundation continued operating at $650,000 to $1.6 million in annual revenue but showed zero grants paid across all eight annual filings from 2016 to 2024, functioning as a dormant or investment-holding vehicle.

A December 23, 2014 charity commitment list prepared by Richard Joslin and sent to Epstein documents giving directed or advised by Epstein to recipients including the Dartmouth Visual Arts Center, Dartmouth President's House Renovation, North Shore LIJ, World Jewish Congress, and Rockefeller University [Finding #27][EFTA02371754]. The Origins Project at Arizona State University, directed by Lawrence Krauss, received substantial donations from both Black personally and the Leon Black Family Foundation; as of early 2019, approximately $607,000 in unused funds remained from those donations, and Krauss was removed as director and the program terminated [Finding #16]. Black wrote a formal letter in December 2014 about the Origins Project, Epstein was separately a donor, and MIT's Joi Ito later confirmed MIT was able to keep Black's money but had to bounce a $25,000 Epstein-foundation gift back to ASU [Finding #16]. The Dechert report noted Black also made donations at Epstein's request to MIT, Harvard, the ASU Origins Project, and the International Peace Institute [Finding #1524]. The Black Foundation gave $200,000 to IPI in December 2014, during a period when IPI was receiving Epstein support through Terje Rod-Larsen [Finding #5]. Cross-reference of the charity commitment list, Dechert's donation summary, and Gratitude America's grant records indicates Epstein functioned as an intermediary directing portions of Black's philanthropic capital toward institutions within his own support network [Finding #1524][Finding #27][Finding #4].

sections.title: Investigations and Legal Proceedings
sections.content:
Multiple investigations have examined the Black-Epstein relationship. The Manhattan District Attorney's office (DANY) investigated Black on trafficking allegations connected to Epstein, identifying at least three victims [Finding #10][EFTA02731082]. One complainant described being instructed by Epstein to massage Black at Epstein's New York residence circa 2011-2012, during which Black "began initiating sexual contact, at which point [she] ran out of the room. [She] complained to Epstein, who laughed" [Finding #10]. Jeanne M. Christensen, partner at Wigdor LLP, represented complainants in the DANY investigation, and LMSBAND records show her co-occurring in 21 documents alongside Black — the highest co-occurrence after Epstein himself [Finding #10]. DANY ultimately closed its investigation as to Black, and Black was not criminally charged [Finding #10]. SDNY was also involved with a U.S. v. Black matter in the record [Finding #10]. The Senate Finance Committee, chaired by Senator Ron Wyden, investigated the Black-Epstein financial relationship and received a formal memorandum from Paul Weiss on Black's behalf [Finding #10][EFTA02731023].

Apollo's Conflicts Committee commissioned Dechert LLP to conduct an independent investigation after October 2020 news coverage reported the scale of Black's payments to Epstein. The Dechert report, filed as Apollo 8-K exhibit EX-99.1 on January 25, 2021, established the $158 million total, the payment timeline, and the advisory scope, and concluded there was no evidence Epstein introduced Black to underage women [Finding #1460][SEC:0001193125-21-016405]. The report acknowledged the payments "far exceeded any amounts Black paid to his other professional advisors" [Finding #1460]. Separately, the HOUSE_OVERSIGHT_023355 advisory-ecosystem list and the August 2016 Form 8865 sequence show Paul Weiss and Apollo's in-house tax function engaged across all three Apollo founders' tax filings, not solely Black's personal advisory bill — a scope that extends beyond the Conflicts Committee's focus on Black as an individual [Finding #1486][Finding #1574]. Black's January 25, 2021 letter to Apollo limited partners announced his retirement as CEO "on or before" his 70th birthday (July 2021), Marc Rowan as successor CEO, cancellation of Class C shares that had given co-founders extra voting rights, and a $200 million pledge toward initiatives "that seek to achieve gender equality and protect and empower women" [Finding #1460]. Apollo engaged WilmerHale for a reputational risk review, hired its first global head of citizenship and first head of enterprise risk management, and established a reputational risk committee. Former SEC Chairman Jay Clayton was appointed Lead Independent Director in February 2021 and Non-Executive Chairman after Black stepped down.

Civil litigation continues. Doe v. Black (1:23-cv-06418, SDNY), a personal injury action filed July 25, 2023, was assigned to Judge Jessica G. L. Clarke and remains pending, with an appeal filed to the Second Circuit (25-564) on March 11, 2025 [Finding #1384]. Separately, Black filed a RICO suit against Guzel Ganieva (Black v. Ganieva, 1:21-cv-08824, SDNY), who had publicly accused him of sexual assault; Black alleged extortion, and that case also reached the Second Circuit. DOJ Volume 11 records document in-person meetings between Epstein and Black multiple times per month from at least 2010 through June 2019, held at Epstein's 9 East 71st Street townhouse and at Black's Apollo office at 9 West 57th Street; post-2008-conviction meetings continued through at least November 2016, including Paris-New York visits by Black to Epstein's residence [Finding #9].

sections.title: Political Activity and Network Position
sections.content:
Black is among the largest political donors in the Epstein network, with over 1,185 FEC contributions on record. Major donations include $100,000 to Right to Rise USA (Jeb Bush, 2015), $100,000 to With Honor Fund (2017), $100,000 to Fighting for Ohio Fund (2016), $100,000 to Senate Majority PAC (2016), and $100,000 to Congressional Leadership Fund (2015). Recent recipients span both parties and include Tim Scott, Chuck Schumer, Tom Cotton, Cory Booker, Susan Collins, David Perdue, Kelly Loeffler, and Thom Tillis. His political giving operates outside the small-donor Epstein bundling patterns observed elsewhere in the investigation, though FEC records show coordinated same-date donations with fellow Apollo co-founders Marc Rowan and Joshua Harris to 15 or more shared recipients including McConnell, Cotton, and Graham — consistent with private equity industry coordination through the American Investment Council.

Epstein served as a meeting broker and social gatekeeper for Black on selected introductions [Finding #24]. Documents show Epstein scheduling a meeting between Black and "Sergey" in November 2015 [Finding #24][EFTA00334966] and listing Black alongside Peter Thiel, Lawrence Summers, Bill Burns, Gordon Brown, Thorbjorn Jagland, and the president of Mongolia in an email to Kathryn Ruemmler about a September 2014 gathering [Finding #24][EFTA02581474]. David Stern reported to Epstein from the Future Investment Initiative in Riyadh in October 2017: "lot of your friends there Leon Black Tom Barrack Sultan," placing Black in the Gulf investment circuit alongside other Epstein associates. Glenn Dubin forwarded a Bloomberg article about Black's tax reform dilemma to Epstein in December 2017, placing Dubin-Epstein-Black in a shared intelligence-sharing chain on Wall Street developments. Nicholas Ribis reported to Epstein on Caesars and Apollo, including a Davis Report that criticized Black and Apollo losses — a reporting pattern that coincided with Ribis receiving financial support from Epstein on the Cal Neva casino deal.

A.B. Krongard, former CIA Executive Director (2001-2004), serves as Independent Director at Apollo Global Management. Separately, Vincenzo Iozzo asked Epstein to facilitate a test of the IperLane surveillance product with Apollo in September 2015: "speaking of Leon Black, it'd be awesome if at some point in the next few months we could do a test run with Apollo once we also have the iOS version ready. I know they currently use one of our competitors" [EFTA02712657]. The email places Epstein as a requested intermediary between a surveillance technology vendor and Apollo, though no Apollo deployment has been confirmed in the record.

sections.title: Post-Epstein Transition and Share Liquidation
sections.content:
The disclosure of the $158 million payment accompanied Apollo's first leadership transition at the founder level [Finding #1460]. Black's January 2021 letter to limited partners tied his CEO retirement to the Epstein relationship: "Having reflected at great length on my professional relationship with Mr. Epstein, a relationship that I profoundly regret" [Finding #1460]. The governance changes included Marc Rowan as successor CEO (unanimously chosen by the Executive Committee and Board), cancellation of Class C shares that had given co-founders extra voting rights, a move to single-class stock, and engagement of WilmerHale for reputational risk review [Finding #1460]. Jay Clayton, former SEC Chairman, was appointed Lead Independent Director and subsequently Non-Executive Chairman. These governance reforms coincided with the Epstein disclosure; broader private equity industry trends and Apollo's succession planning were concurrent factors.
